summary: Shares experience from using ISO 8613, the Office Document Architecture (ODA), to translate multimedia information. It is meant for implementors considering ODA as a format for multimedia mail and file exchange. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some people tried a document format for pictures and text together. They wrote down what went well and badly to help others.

questions: what is oda for multimedia mail
how do you exchange multimedia documents
subtitle: Lessons from using ISO ODA for multimedia document exchange

tldr.problem: ISO Office Document Architecture (ODA) was being proposed as a format for multimedia mail and file exchange, but it was a complex, abstract standard and implementors needed practical guidance.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reports the findings of the EXPRES project, a collaborative effort between Carnegie Mellon and University of Michigan (with vendors) that investigated using ODA to exchange research proposals via email, documenting strategies and lessons learned.
tldr.outcome: The project demonstrated that ODA could work for multimedia interchange but required a concrete document application profile (DAP) to define common entities like paragraphs and provide mapping to existing systems.

today: RFC 1197 is Informational, documenting the EXPRES project findings. ODA saw limited adoption in practice. Today's multimedia and document interchange instead relies on formats like HTML, PDF, and modern email MIME types.

sections.title: ISO Office Document Architecture
sections.content:
The ISO 8613 standard for Office Document Architecture (ODA) defines a way to represent documents containing multifont text, raster images and geometric graphics. ODA was also standardized by CCITT as T.410 and was being considered for use in email and file exchange systems.

However, ODA is highly abstract, defining complex entities like "composite logical object classes" rather than concepts users understand, such as paragraphs. This abstraction made ODA difficult to use without additional guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: ODA is a very detailed blueprint for how to describe pictures and text, but it is so complicated that people needed help using it.

sections.title: The EXPRES Project
sections.content:
The National Science Foundation funded the EXPRES project to investigate practical use of ODA for exchanging research proposals via electronic mail. Teams from Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Michigan collaborated with McDonnell-Douglas Aerospace Information Systems, NIST, and Interleaf.

The groups developed strategies for using ODA based on the NIST document application profile (DAP) and features provided by real systems (Andrew, Diamond, and Interleaf). These experiences were documented in a published book.
sections.plainLanguage: A group of universities and companies worked together to figure out how to actually use ODA for sending documents through email.

sections.title: Key Findings
sections.content:
The RFC references a book that documents the EXPRES findings, describing strategies for using ODA and lessons from the implementation work. The group's discussion of what worked and what did not is intended to be valuable for others considering ODA as an interchange format.

The main lesson is that a document application profile (DAP) is essential: it must define common, recognizable concepts and provide clear mapping between ODA entities and the formats used in systems that want to interchange documents.
sections.plainLanguage: To make ODA actually work, you have to create a simpler profile that defines real things like "paragraph" and "heading" that people understand.

references.text: Rosenberg, J., Sherman, M., Marks, A. & Akkerhuis, J., "Multi-media Document Translation: ODA and the EXPRES Project", Springer-Verlag, 1991.
